One-sentence judgment: broadcast technicians do not "watch machines"; they set up, operate, and maintain the electronic equipment used to capture, edit, and transmit audio and video, control and adjust the outgoing and incoming broadcast signal (volume, signal strength, and clarity), operate satellite, microwave, or transmitting equipment to broadcast programs, monitor transmitter readings, and handle abnormalities according to procedures. On the U.S. side this corresponds to O*NET-SOC 27-4012.00, listed as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to below 7.0). The core boundary is this: you may stand watch over the link according to the plan, adjust parameters, service equipment, and record readings, but you cannot replace program content decisions and compliance review, nor use others' works, record others' performances, or use material beyond the authorized scope without obtaining a license.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to look at the signal flow and the equipment manual before acting, can monitor indicators for long periods and record readings faithfully; your interest in "is the link redundant, can an interruption be recovered quickly, are the parameters within the allowed range" is greater than in "was today's broadcast lively"; and when the equipment is abnormal, an indicator exceeds its limit, or a power outage is needed for servicing, you are willing to stop and report along the escalation chain rather than letting the program go out degraded.

Conditions for pausing high investment: you have not yet completed one full cycle under mentoring from link checking, equipment status confirmation, parameter adjustment, broadcast watch duty, and abnormality handling through to records and handover, or you only want to operate equipment and are unwilling to learn the procedures and records; also do not treat "knowing how to build a computer" or "having seen a mixing console" as proof that you can stand watch over a broadcast link independently.

Education, qualifications, and position authorization must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), and the education composition includes three categories: a bachelor's degree, an associate or other two-year degree, and a high school diploma or equivalent; in mainland China, the site selection, design, construction, and installation of radio and television transmission coverage network projects must be undertaken by units that have obtained the corresponding qualification certificates according to law, the completed project must pass acceptance before being put into use, and transmitting stations and relay stations must operate according to the approved technical parameters; the specific position's equipment operating authorization and servicing authority are determined by the employing unit and the competent department's rules.

One sentence: this is a technical position centered on equipment setup and maintenance, signal transmission and reception and parameter adjustment, transmitting and transmission watch duty, troubleshooting, and records, and its output is a reproducible broadcast signal and traceable equipment and reading records, not program content or commercial decisions. The U.S. wage, employment, and projection data are the Broadcast Technicians (SOC 27-4012) occupational basis; the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook's Broadcast, Sound, and Video Technicians is a broader group basis that also covers audio and video technicians (27-4011) and sound engineering technicians (27-4014); mainland China, following the evidence routing, does not publish this occupation's occupational-level or industry proxy wage values and retains only the basis and the gap.

The work of this occupation can be divided into three categories: first, setup and maintenance (installing and configuring equipment according to the plan, maintaining the in-station computers and network, performing calibration and routine maintenance according to the manual, and recording equipment status and servicing); second, watch duty and adjustment (monitoring the outgoing and incoming signal and the monitors, adjusting volume, signal strength, and clarity, adjusting video fidelity and brightness and contrast, playing and recording programs through the automation system, and monitoring and recording transmitter readings); third, abnormality handling and handover (reporting equipment problems immediately and ensuring that repair is carried out, performing emergency repairs when necessary, switching to a backup link along the escalation chain, and filling in the duty and reading records and handing over). All three share the same traceable chain of equipment and signal records.
Setup and maintenance

Check the broadcast plan and the link diagram → confirm the power, grounding, and interface conditions → install and configure the equipment and perform calibration → maintain the in-station computers and network → perform routine maintenance and inspection according to the manual → register the equipment status and servicing records.
Watch duty and signal adjustment

Monitor the signal and the monitors according to the broadcast schedule → adjust the volume, signal strength, and clarity → adjust video fidelity and brightness and contrast → play and record programs through the automation system → monitor and record transmitter readings → communicate levels and broadcast status with in-station positions.

Report equipment problems immediately and track the repair to completion, performing an emergency repair or switching to a backup link when necessary; fill in the duty record and the transmitter reading sheet, organize the equipment change and fault handling notes, and hand over unclosed items and risk notes to the next shift.

Broadcast technicians focus on the broadcast equipment link, watch duty, and troubleshooting; announcers and DJs focus on content expression; AV focuses on event audio and video systems; sound engineering also covers recording and live sound and cannot be limited to the studio; network support can also serve broadcast IP systems but requires additional signal and station procedure training. The telecommunications and electronics engineering directions emphasize their own design tasks more, and duties and authorization are checked by position.
Core purpose

On the premise of meeting the power, grounding, and equipment procedure requirements, keep the broadcast signal stable, clear, switchable, and reproducible at each link of capture, editing, and transmission, and keep the equipment status, parameter adjustments, and fault handling as traceable records.
Main objects and basis

The objects are the electronic equipment for capturing, editing, and transmitting audio and video, the transmitting and transmission equipment, the in-station computers and network, and the monitors, consoles, and reading records; the basis is the broadcast plan and link diagram, the equipment manuals and technical standards, the unit's operating and servicing procedures, and the content licensing and safe broadcast requirements.
Core process

Plan and link checking, equipment installation and configuration, signal monitoring and parameter adjustment, program playback and recording, transmitter reading monitoring and recording, fault reporting and emergency handling, servicing and maintenance, and record handover.
Main outputs

A stable, reproducible broadcast signal and a switchable link, equipment configuration and servicing records, transmitter readings and duty records, fault handling and change notes, and an updated equipment ledger and operating parameter baseline.
Responsible party

Article 22 of the current Regulations on the Administration of Radio and Television in China: the site selection, design, construction, and installation of transmission coverage network projects are handled according to state rules and undertaken by units that have obtained the corresponding qualification certificates according to law; on completion the radio and television administrative department organizes acceptance, and only after passing may it be put into use. Article 20: approved frequencies and bands may not be leased or transferred, and approved technical parameters may not be changed without authorization. Routine internal configuration review does not equal statutory project acceptance. Daily technical work, program arrangements, crews, and contractors cooperate according to their real duties, and final decision authority is not obtained automatically through the occupational name.
Authority and approval

Link switching, internal configuration, and outage servicing follow the actual authorization, the contingency plan, and the equipment requirements; a training record does not automatically grant operating authority, and a change to an approved transmitting technical parameter additionally requires checking the regulatory requirement in Article 20.
Boundary of conclusions

The record states "what parameters and handling this shift watched over and recorded according to the plan"; it does not equal zero broadcast interruption, nor does it replace the compliance conclusion on project acceptance and safe broadcasting, and it is affected by equipment aging, external links, and temporary scheduling.

Before starting the job, check at least six items: the position basis and form of employment (full-time, shift work, outsourced operations, or project-based), the actual working hours (the frequency of night, weekend, and holiday duty), the equipment and safety training arrangements, the scope of authorization for electricity, work at height, and transmitting equipment, the use restrictions on materials and signals, and the real method of pay (monthly salary, shift allowance, or project settlement) and the overtime settlement rules.
Occupational basis

This page's precise O*NET27-4012, media occupational group. Current O*NET 2025 industry shares: information 70%, other 30% (including education and arts, entertainment, and recreation); this is the U.S. 27-4012 structure and does not lead to Chinese employment, specific industry headcounts, or wages. The BLS combined group contains four sub-items: AV, broadcast, sound, and lighting, and also has separately listed wages and projections. The one-to-one Chinese mapping has not been verified, so no claim is made that a particular detailed category exists or that no detailed category exists at all.
Education and training path

The O*NET education answers mark a bachelor's degree, an associate or other two-year degree, and a high school equivalent as "requirements for some positions," without giving percentages, and they are not the education composition of current workers. Job Zone3/SVP6 to <7 is an occupational group preparation summary; the precise BLS 27-4012 typical entry is an associate degree, no related work experience required, and short-term on-the-job training, with the specific employer checked separately.
Methods and tools

The details page's 11 software categories and the Hot single page's 13 products are different counts; 2025 hiring mentions are Office9%, Excel6%, Outlook, Linux, and PowerPoint 3% each, Word2%, AutoCAD, Photoshop, and Windows 1% each, AfterEffects and UNIX <1%, and Illustrator and InDesign have no ratio; the top two are InDemand and are not a deployment, efficiency, or substitution rate. On-site equipment, servers, and measuring instruments are checked against the actual position configuration.
Safety and work permits

Check the electricity, radio frequency, and height risks against the actual equipment and work, and do not automatically treat all equipment rooms or battery rooms as confined spaces. Special operations within the Chinese catalog require the corresponding valid operating certificate, and the unit verifies authenticity; ordinary wiring is not automatically counted as electrician or work-at-height special operations because of the occupational name. U.S. OSHA1910.333 on de-energizing, lockout and tagging, and testing by a qualified person applies only under that clause's conditions; China follows the applicable rules and unit procedures. Night shift and fatigue arrangements are checked against the real roster, and 96% working 40 hours per week cannot prove night shift work.
Training and regulatory requirements

Article 22 of the current Regulations on the Administration of Radio and Television in China: the site selection, design, construction, and installation of transmission coverage network projects are handled according to state rules and undertaken by units that have obtained the corresponding qualification certificates according to law; on completion the radio and television administrative department organizes acceptance, and only after passing may it be put into use. Article 20: approved frequencies and bands may not be leased or transferred, and approved technical parameters may not be changed without authorization. Routine internal configuration review does not equal statutory project acceptance. Article 46 of the Copyright Law has a specific exception limited to radio and television stations: playing another's unpublished work requires a license and remuneration, while published works may be played without a license but with remuneration as provided; it cannot be applied directly to ordinary online publishing. Article 45 on remuneration for public communication of sound recordings, and the recording of performances and the making of recordings, are different rights and exceptions checked separately, and a unit's license list cannot cover all acts with one item.
Pay and work hours

Editorial contract verification: duty, standby, allowances, outsourcing, and project settlement must be checked against the real arrangements; no hiring frequency for this occupation was collected, so no claim is made that a particular method of pay or employment is universal.

Broadcast technicians (U.S. side O*NET-SOC 27-4012.00, Broadcast Technicians) set up, operate, and maintain the electronic equipment used to capture, edit, and transmit audio and video, serving radio and television programs; they control and adjust the outgoing and incoming broadcast signal to regulate volume, signal strength, and clarity; and they operate satellite, microwave, or other transmitting equipment to broadcast programs. Daily work includes playing and recording programs through the automation system, monitoring the strength and clarity of the outgoing and incoming signal and adjusting equipment, watching the monitors and communicating audio and video levels and broadcast status with in-station personnel, monitoring and recording transmitter readings, adjusting the fidelity and brightness and contrast of video transmission, setting up and maintaining the in-station computers and network, and installing equipment and troubleshooting and performing minor repairs. The complete task list also includes program replacement Core74, electronic editing Core73, graphics Supplemental77, and scripts and training films Supplemental54 and content reporting 51; technicians are not excluded across the board from content work, and final broadcast review and scheduling authority are checked separately against the organization's duties.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 27-4012.00 Broadcast Technicians, page updated 2026, Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), and this occupation is not marked Bright Outlook. The official duties are to "set up, operate, and maintain the electronic equipment used to capture, edit, and transmit audio and video for radio or television programs; control and adjust the outgoing and incoming broadcast signal to regulate volume, signal strength, and clarity; and operate satellite, microwave, or other transmitting equipment to broadcast radio or television programs"; there are 28 tasks in total, and the highly important tasks include playing and recording programs through the automation system (88), reporting equipment problems and ensuring repair is carried out and performing emergency repairs when necessary (88), setting up and maintaining the in-station computers and network (87), watching the monitors and confirming audio and video levels and broadcast status with in-station personnel (85), and monitoring the strength and clarity of the outgoing and incoming signal and adjusting equipment (85). There are 28 tasks in total, 19 Core and 9 Supplemental; there are also 41 general activities, 25 detailed activities, and 57 work context items, each counted separately.

U.S. wage distribution: the 2025 BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) presented by O*NET, on the basis of Broadcast Technicians (SOC 27-4012) — annual wage 10th percentile 31,390 USD, 25th percentile 40,320 USD, median 59,570 USD, 75th percentile 83,520 USD, and 90th percentile 123,670 USD; the corresponding hourly wages are 15.09, 19.38, 28.64, 40.16, and 59.46 USD.

Insufficient evidence: no national Chinese wage distribution or one-to-one corresponding detailed category mapping for this occupation has been obtained. Background reference: in 2025 the culture, sports, and entertainment industry was 129447 for urban non-private units and 64015 yuan per year pre-tax for private units (NBS); the sector mixes many positions, does not represent broadcast technicians or the actual industry classification of all stations, and no starting or monthly wage is inferred.

paragraphs: This page compares broadcast technicians with five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and output, key differences, and which direction suits each preference. The adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupational descriptions and do not mean the trade names are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career directions and core outputs are based on the official descriptions of O*NET 27-4012.00 and adjacent entries (27-3011.00, 27-4011.00, and 27-4014.00 each taken from their O*NET official pages) and are on the U.S. basis; the qualification, authorization, and broadcast requirements of adjacent trades must be verified separately by their own jurisdiction, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut to a career change.

The table below compares the direction differences between broadcast technicians and adjacent trades; the basis for judgment is the main output, what the role is responsible for, and the training required, rather than how similar the trade names are.
Broadcast Announcers and Radio Disc Jockeys (27-3011.00)
Announce, link, and interview according to the script and the run sheet, with broadcast content and the program log as the main output.

Announcers and disc jockeys face scripts and spoken expression and are responsible for the content; broadcast technicians face equipment and the signal link and are responsible for stable broadcasting and for parameters and records.
If you would rather do content expression, look first at broadcast announcers and radio disc jockeys; if you would rather work on equipment and links, look first at broadcast technicians.
Audio and Video Technicians (27-4011.00)
Set up, operate, and strike audio and video equipment for live or recorded events, with on-site signals and test records as the main output.

Audio and video technicians face events and recording sites and need on-site safety work such as electricity and rigging; broadcast technicians face the in-station broadcast link and the transmitting and transmission equipment and stand watch under the duty system.

If you would rather follow events and the site, look first at audio and video technicians; if you would rather guard the broadcast link and the transmitting station, look first at broadcast technicians.
Sound Engineering Technicians (27-4014.00)
Responsible for in-studio pickup, mixing, and mastering, with finished recordings and project files as the main output.

Sound engineering technicians center on acoustics and the mixing bus and work mainly in the recording studio; broadcast technicians center on the signal chain, the transmitting and transmission equipment, and network maintenance.
If you would rather polish the finished sound, look first at sound engineering technicians; if you would rather handle links and equipment, look first at broadcast technicians.
Computer Network Support Specialists
Provide support and troubleshooting for office and business networks, with usable network and system environments as the main output.

Network support faces office and business systems and handles accounts, systems, and network connectivity; broadcast technicians face the broadcast link and the transmitting and transmission equipment and must follow the safe broadcast and duty procedures.

If you would rather do general network support, look first at computer network support specialists; if you would rather work on broadcast and transmission equipment, look first at broadcast technicians.
Telecommunications Engineering Specialists
Design and optimize communications networks and transmission systems, with plans, test reports, and operating systems as the main output.

Telecommunications engineering centers on system design and transmission technology and usually requires deeper professional training; broadcast technicians center on watch duty, maintenance, and troubleshooting of the equipment in the live network.

If you would rather do network and transmission design, look first at telecommunications engineering specialists; if you would rather do equipment watch duty and servicing, look first at broadcast technicians.
Electronics Engineers, Except Computer
Design electronic circuits and systems and perform verification testing, with design documents and test reports as the main output.
Electronics engineers center on circuit and system design and need the corresponding professional training; broadcast technicians center on configuring, operating, and repairing finished equipment.
If you would rather do circuit and system design, look first at electronics engineers; if you would rather do equipment operations and troubleshooting, look first at broadcast technicians.

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the main output, what the role is responsible for, and the training required, not how similar the names are; once the direction is set, check the target position's equipment system and duty system, the actual shifts and time slots, the authorization arrangements for electricity and work-at-height, and the confidentiality and use agreements for equipment and signals item by item, and keep written confirmation.

paragraphs: Students or career changers preparing to enter this occupation

Editorial study suggestion: first use a paper or offline fictional link to practice parameter checking, fault hypotheses, and record handover. Supervised practical training requires first checking suitable training, the necessary qualifications, and the unit's equipment authorization; special operations within the catalog require meeting the applicable certification conditions before going on the job, and a real task cannot be done first and the certificate obtained later. Whether the target position is at a radio station, television station, transmitting station, online platform, or equipment vendor, their rules, equipment authorization, and safety requirements must be checked separately.
Practicing broadcast technicians

Use digital tools in reviewable links such as equipment ledger and parameter baseline management, transmitter reading and duty record compilation, fault work order and spare parts management, and link topology and configuration version comparison; parameter judgment, abnormality decisions, emergency handling, and outage servicing work must still rest with people.
Broadcasting units and operations and maintenance teams

Before introducing tools, clarify the links where they may be used, the knowledge scope for equipment and link data, the authorization boundary for electricity and work-at-height, and the responsible person for recording and review, so that any output returns to a traceable configuration baseline, reading record, and servicing record.
Education and development

Focus training on the signal chain and equipment principles, measurement and calibration methods, the fault location sequence, the safety procedures for transmitting and transmission equipment, and record and handover habits, and also train the habit of checking tool output and the awareness to report abnormalities.

BLS explicitly notes that technology, including AI, may reduce the number of technicians needed to set up and operate broadcast systems; it cannot be guaranteed that tasks such as fault judgment will never change, nor can this occupation's AI substitution rate be derived from the overall projection. entries.answer: Build, operate, and maintain the electronic equipment used to capture, edit, and transmit audio and video: verify chains and power supply and grounding, install and configure equipment, monitor incoming and outgoing signals and monitors and adjust volume, signal strength, and clarity, play and record programs using automated systems, monitor and record transmitter readings, set up and maintain in-station computers and networks, troubleshoot equipment faults and carry out emergency repairs and routine servicing, and complete records and handovers per shift.
entries.question: What does a broadcast technician do every day?

entries.answer: Risks to note in advance include broadcast interruption caused by equipment and chain failures, work-at-height and radio frequency and electrical risks in transmitting and antenna-feed systems, equipment damage and out-of-range indicators caused by improper parameters or grounding, fatigue from night and continuous watch duty, and leakage of equipment and chain information and materials; control depends on operating plans and watch-duty rules, item-by-item confirmation and measurement, qualified personnel performing electrical and work-at-height tasks, and anomaly reporting and escalation procedures.
entries.question: What risks does this job most need to note in advance?

entries.answer: A fit signal is being able to complete watch duty per procedures and record truthfully, to stop first and report along the escalation chain when indicators are out of range or equipment is abnormal, and to judge chain status from measurement results rather than impressions; an interest in equipment alone is not enough to prove competence.

entries.answer: Steps such as equipment ledgers and parameter baselines, reading aggregation, work order and spare-parts management, and configuration version comparison can be assisted; parameter judgment, fault isolation, emergency handling, de-energized maintenance, and broadcast responsibility remain with people.
